problem: Session 114 established that a container's writable layer is thin, on top of read-only image layers. What it didn't dwell on: that writable layer is disposable. Stop and remove the ethics-db container from Session 115's lab, and every row Postgres wrote to disk inside that container is gone with it — there is no undo.

This is exactly the failure mode that makes containers unsuitable for stateful data by default, and exactly the problem container storage solves: how do you keep data that must outlive a container's restart, redeploy, or crash, while still getting all the packaging and portability benefits from Session 114?
concept: Container storage is about deciding, for every piece of data a container touches, whether it should live and die with that specific container instance, or persist independently of it. Docker gives you three mechanisms, each with a different lifecycle:

Mechanism Lifecycle Typical use Container writable layer Dies with the container Temp files, caches — anything truly disposable Volume Managed by Docker, persists until explicitly removed Databases, anything that must survive container removal Bind mount Lives on the host filesystem at a path you choose Local dev — sharing source code live into a container The rule of thumb: if data needs to survive `docker rm`, it does not belong in the container's writable layer. It belongs in a volume.
deep: Volumes — Docker-managed persistence A volume is a directory, managed entirely by Docker, that lives outside any single container's writable layer — by default under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ on Linux. Docker handles its lifecycle: it's created explicitly (or implicitly on first use), and it survives docker rm on the container that used it. Multiple containers can mount the same volume simultaneously.

docker volume create ethics-db-data docker run -d --name ethics-db \ -v ethics-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ --network ethics-net postgres:16 # Remove and recreate the container -- data is untouched:

docker rm -f ethics-db docker run -d --name ethics-db \ -v ethics-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ --network ethics-net postgres:16 # Same data is there -- the volume, not the container, owned it Bind mounts — host-controlled paths A bind mount maps a specific path on the host directly into the container. Unlike a volume, Docker doesn't manage its lifecycle at all — it's just a path, and it exists precisely as long as the host directory does. This makes it ideal for local development (edit code on the host, see it live inside the running container) and risky for anything else, since the container now depends on host filesystem structure that may not exist on a different machine.

docker run -d --name triage-dev \ -v "$(pwd)/src:/app/src" \ ethics-triage:1.0 # Edits to ./src on the host appear inside /app/src instantly -- # no rebuild needed. Great for dev, wrong for production.

tmpfs mounts — the third, less common option A tmpfs mount stores data in host memory only, never touching disk — useful for short-lived sensitive data (like a decrypted credential used briefly during a job) that you explicitly do not want persisted anywhere, even accidentally.
workflow: Applied to the ethics-db container introduced in Session 115, deciding what needs persistence versus what doesn't:
1. Identify every path inside the container that holds data you can't afford to lose: for Postgres, that's /var/lib/postgresql/data.
2. Create a named volume for it: docker volume create ethics-db-data.
3. Mount it at container creation, never after: -v ethics-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data.

4. Anything NOT mounted to a volume (temp files, logs written inside the container, package caches) is implicitly disposable — treat it that way, and don't build logic that assumes it survives a restart.

5. For local development against the same setup, use a bind mount for source code only (so edits are instant) while still using a named volume for the database data — mixing the two mechanisms for their respective strengths is normal and expected.

6. Before ever running docker rm on a stateful container, confirm the data lives in a named volume, not the container's writable layer — this single check prevents the most common Docker data-loss incident.
enterprise: On a single host, Docker volumes are simple local directories. At enterprise/cluster scale, 'container storage' becomes its own subsystem, because a container can now be rescheduled onto a different physical machine entirely — and the data has to follow it.

Scale Storage mechanism Single host Docker named volumes, local disk Multi-host cluster (Kubernetes) PersistentVolumes backed by network storage (NFS, cloud disks) so any node can attach them Cloud Managed block storage (e.g. Persistent Disk, EBS) or managed databases entirely, bypassing container storage altogether This is the strongest argument, in real enterprise practice, for NOT containerizing a database at all once you're past a small internal tool: run the database as a managed cloud service (Cloud SQL, RDS) and keep containers stateless, delegating persistence to infrastructure purpose-built for it. Container storage matters most for small, self-contained tools — exactly the CEx tooling context this Knowledge Map keeps anchoring to.
dependencies: The host filesystem and its storage driver (overlay2), which underlies both the container's writable layer and where Docker physically stores volume data.
Sufficient host disk space — volumes are not magically infinite; docker system df shows real usage.
For multi-host setups, a network storage backend (NFS, cloud block storage) so a volume can be reattached if a container is rescheduled elsewhere.
Backup tooling external to Docker itself — Docker does not back up volumes for you; that's a separate operational responsibility (tying to Layer 5, Session 78, Backup).
dependents: Any stateful containerized service — databases, message queues, anything that can't lose data on restart — depends entirely on correct volume usage.

Kubernetes PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims (Layer 8, Session 119) are the direct, cluster-scale evolution of exactly this concept.
Backup and disaster-recovery processes (Layer 5, Sessions 78, 80) — you can't back up what you haven't correctly identified as persistent in the first place.
security: Risk Mitigation Sensitive data written to the container's writable layer by mistake Explicitly volume-mount any path that holds sensitive or important data Bind-mounting sensitive host directories unintentionally Mount the narrowest possible path, never a broad directory like the home folder or root Volume left behind after container removal, containing sensitive data docker volume rm explicitly when a volume is genuinely done, and audit docker volume ls periodically No backup of volume data Treat volumes holding real data exactly like a production disk — back it up on a schedule Read-write access granted where read-only would do Add :ro to bind mounts and volumes that a container only needs to read from For anything touching KYC or refund data specifically: prefer not persisting sensitive data inside a container's storage at all if a managed database service is available — it inherits that service's encryption-at-rest, access controls, and backup posture instead of requiring you to reimplement all of it yourself at the Docker volume level.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Command Data disappeared after docker rm Data was in the writable layer, not a volume docker volume ls (confirm no volume existed) "no space left on device" Host disk full, often from unpruned volumes/images docker system df Bind mount shows empty directory in container Host path doesn't exist or was mistyped ls the host path before mounting Permission denied writing to a mounted volume UID/GID mismatch between container process and volume ownership docker exec <container> id;

check volume file ownership Changes to a bind-mounted file not appearing in container Editor's save process breaks the bind (some editors replace-on-save) Check host file's inode; some tools recreate rather than edit files Volume persists after container and image are removed Expected — volumes have an independent lifecycle by design docker volume rm <name> explicitly if truly done docker volume ls and docker volume inspect <name> answer the two questions that come up constantly: 'does this data actually live in a volume,' and 'where on the host disk is it physically stored.'
example: Continuing the 3-container pattern from Session 115: the database container's volume is exactly the kind of thing that shows up in an incident postmortem when it's gotten wrong. A common real-world mistake is a well-meaning cleanup script running docker system prune -a --volumes on a production host, silently deleting every unused volume including ones that turn out not to have been truly unused.

Pattern to notice docker system prune with the --volumes flag is destructive and irreversible. Enterprises that have been burned by this typically ban that flag from any automated script and require an explicit, reviewed step before any volume is ever deleted in production.
cloud: Cloud container platforms generally push you away from container-managed storage and toward purpose-built managed storage services, precisely because containers are meant to be disposable and easily rescheduled — state fights against that.

Platform Storage approach Google Cloud Run Stateless by design — no persistent local disk; use Cloud SQL or Cloud Storage instead Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) PersistentVolumeClaims backed by Persistent Disk AWS ECS/Fargate EFS-backed volumes for Fargate; EBS for EC2-backed tasks Managed databases generally Cloud SQL, RDS, etc. — sidestep container storage for the database tier entirely Given CEx's existing Google-based stack, the realistic long-term shape for any tool that grows out of Apps Script is a stateless Cloud Run container talking to Cloud SQL or Firestore, rather than a container carrying its own volume — container storage as covered in this session is primarily a local-development and small-single-host concern.
automation: docker-compose declares volumes the same declarative way it declares networks, making persistence part of the same reproducible file as everything else:
- ./src:/app/src:ro # bind mount, dev-only, read-only ports: ["8080:80"] networks: [cex-net] volumes:

Backup automation for a Docker volume typically runs as a separate, short-lived container that mounts the same volume read-only and streams it to storage — e.g. a nightly job container that tars up ethics- db-data and uploads it to Cloud Storage, tying directly back to Layer 5's Backup session.
career: Storage is where junior container knowledge often stops short — most tutorials cover running a stateless web app, few walk through the data-loss trap of an unvolumed database. Being able to explain, unprompted, why a database container needs a named volume and why docker system prune --volumes is dangerous in production is a reliable signal of real operational experience, not just tutorial completion.
It also connects cleanly to backup/DR concepts (Layer 5) that show up constantly in sysadmin and SRE interviews — 'how do you back up a containerized database' is a very common practical question.

misconceptions: Misconception Reality Data inside a container is safe as long as the container exists True only until docker rm — the writable layer is not durable storage Volumes and bind mounts are interchangeable Volumes are Docker-managed and portable; bind mounts depend on a specific host path Docker automatically backs up volumes It does not — backup is a separate, manual or scripted responsibility Removing a container also removes its volumes Volumes have an independent lifecycle and persist until explicitly removed Containerizing a database is always the right production choice Managed database services are often the safer, lower- operational-burden choice
anchors: Writable layer = a sticky note. Volume = a filing cabinet. Only one of them survives you throwing away the desk (the container).
Bind mount = 'this exact host folder, mapped in.' Volume = 'Docker, you manage where this lives.'
If it needs to survive `docker rm`, it needs a volume — no exceptions.
`docker system prune --volumes` is the container-world equivalent of `rm -rf` on a production disk.

lab: Hands-on: prove to yourself, concretely, the difference between the writable layer and a volume, using the ethics-db container from Session 115.
14. Start a Postgres container WITHOUT a volume: docker run -d --name test-db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass postgres:16.
15. Connect and insert a row of test data.
16. Remove the container: docker rm -f test-db, then start a fresh one with the same name and image — confirm the data is gone.
17. Now repeat with a named volume: docker volume create ethics-db-data, and run Postgres with - v ethics-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data.
18. Insert the same test row, remove the container, start a new one mounting the SAME volume, and confirm the data survived.
19. Run docker volume inspect ethics-db-data and note the Mountpoint field — the actual host path where this data physically lives.
20. Simulate a backup: run a short-lived container that mounts ethics-db-data read-only and tars its contents to a file on the host.
21. Clean up test-only volumes explicitly with docker volume rm — never with a blanket --volumes prune, to build the right habit.

Production tie-in Steps 4–7 are the exact pattern you'd use for the ethics-db container from Session 115's lab if it needed to survive redeploys — and the backup step is the minimum viable version of what a real nightly backup job container would do.
